meta.title: Georgian (ქართული ენა) Language Ontology
meta.description: A comprehensive ontology of the Georgian language (ISO 639-3: kat), the only literary language of the Kartvelian (South Caucasian) family. Georgian is an agglutinative-fusional language with a highly complex verbal system, characterized by poly-personal agreement, split ergativity, and a rich system of preverbs and screeves (tense-aspect-mood paradigms). It is spoken primarily in Georgia and uses the unique Mkhedruli script.
sources: Hewitt, B. G. (2005). Georgian: A Learner's Grammar (2nd ed.). Routledge.
Aronson, H. I. (1990). Georgian: A Reading Grammar. Slavica Publishers.
Kiziria, D. (2009). Beginner's Georgian. Hippocrene Books.
Vogt, H. (1971). Grammaire de la langue géorgienne. Universitetsforlaget.
Shanidze, A. (1973). Kartuli enis gramatikis safuZvlebi (Fundamentals of the Grammar of the Georgian Language). Tbilisi State University Press.
Tschenkeli, K. (1958). Einführung in die georgische Sprache. Amirani Verlag.
meta.speaker_population: Approximately 4 million in Georgia, plus significant communities in Turkey, Russia, Iran, Azerbaijan, and diaspora communities.
meta.location: Georgia (official language), Turkey (northeastern regions), Russia, Iran, Azerbaijan, and diaspora communities.

dialects.name: Kartlian (ქართლური)
dialects.notes: Forms the basis of the standard literary language.

dialects.name: Kakhetian (კახური)
dialects.notes: Close to Kartlian; some phonological and lexical differences.

dialects.name: Imeretian (იმერული)
dialects.notes: Significant differences in verb morphology and phonology.

dialects.name: Gurian (გურული)
dialects.notes: Further phonological reductions; some unique vocabulary.

dialects.name: Adjarian (აჭარული)
dialects.notes: Influenced by Turkish; distinct phonological features.

dialects.name: Meskhetian (მესხური)
dialects.notes: Archaic features; influenced by Armenian and Turkish.

dialects.name: Mountain dialects (Khevsureti, Pshavi, Tusheti, etc.)
dialects.notes: Archaic features, unique vocabulary, and complex consonant clusters.

meta.standard_dialect: Based on the Kartlian dialect, with significant influence from the literary tradition centered in Tbilisi.

Language.definition: Georgian (ქართული ენა) is the official language of the Republic of Georgia and the only literary language of the Kartvelian (South Caucasian) language family. It is an agglutinative-fusional language with a highly complex verbal system, characterized by poly-personal agreement, split ergativity, and a rich system of preverbs and screeves (tense-aspect-mood paradigms). It is spoken primarily in Georgia and uses the unique Mkhedruli script, which is phonemic and has no capital letters.
key_properties: Agglutinative-fusional morphology with complex suffixation and prefixation
Poly-personal verb agreement (subject, direct object, indirect object)
Split ergativity: nominative-accusative in Series I, ergative-absolutive in Series II and III
Seven nominal cases (nominative, ergative, dative, genitive, instrumental, adverbial, vocative)
Rich system of preverbs indicating direction and aspect
Unique Mkhedruli script (33 letters, no capitals)
Complex consonant clusters (up to 6 consonants initially)
Free word order (SOV is basic, but pragmatically flexible)

Lexicon.definition: The inventory of sign units in Georgian, including native Kartvelian roots and loanwords from Iranian, Arabic, Turkish, Russian, and English.
Lexicon.details: The lexicon includes nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, postpositions, particles, numerals, and ideophones. Many basic words are native Kartvelian, but there are extensive borrowings from Iranian languages (Old and Middle Persian), Arabic, Turkish, Russian, and more recently English.

Grammar.definition: The set of rules for operating on these units.
Grammar.details: Includes rules for complex nominal and verbal inflection, poly-personal agreement, split ergativity, preverbation, vowel syncope, and consonant alternations.

Language.definition: The abstract linguistic system in the minds of speakers.
Language.details: The standardized grammatical rules and vocabulary of Georgian, as presented in grammars and used in formal communication.

Speech.definition: The concrete realization of language in communication.
Speech.details: Variants include dialectal differences (e.g., Kartlian, Imeretian, Gurian, Adjarian) and colloquial speech patterns, such as the dropping of final vowels and consonant reductions.

Linguistic_System.definition: Georgian is characterized by a system of 5 vowels and 28 consonants, a rich system of suffixes and prefixes that perform both grammatical and derivational functions, and a complex system of screeves (tense-aspect-mood paradigms).
Linguistic_System.system_of_systems: Georgian can be described as a 'system of systems' with hierarchically ordered levels: phonology, morphology, syntax, and semantics.

Linguistic_Taxon.definition: Georgian is a member of the Kartvelian language family, which is not demonstrably related to any other language family.
Linguistic_Taxon.notes: Within the Kartvelian family, Georgian is most closely related to Mingrelian and Laz (which form the Zan branch), while Svan is more distantly related.

Taxon.definition: Georgian belongs to the Kartvelian language family, which is considered an isolate family.

Genetic_Taxon.definition: Georgian is a Kartvelian language, with no conclusive demonstration of genetic relationship to any other language family.
Genetic_Taxon.genetic_notes: The Kartvelian family is considered one of the oldest language families in the Caucasus. Georgian has been a literary language since the 5th century AD.

Context_of_Use_Taxon.definition: Georgian is used in a variety of contexts, including official, educational, literary, and daily communication.
contexts: Official: Used as the state language of the Republic of Georgia.
Literary/Standard: Based on the Kartlian dialect, used in government, media, and literature.
Daily communication: Used by all generations in all domains of life.
Religious: Used in religious contexts by the Georgian Orthodox Church.
Oral tradition: Rich folklore, including epics and polyphonic folk songs.

Geographic_Taxon.definition: Georgian is spoken in the Republic of Georgia and in diaspora communities.
Geographic_Taxon.area: Republic of Georgia: 69,700 km². Significant diaspora in Turkey, Russia, Iran, Azerbaijan, and other countries.

Political_Taxon.definition: Georgian is the national and official language of the Republic of Georgia.
Political_Taxon.political_status: Official language of the Republic of Georgia. It is also spoken as a minority language in Turkey, Russia, and Iran.

Endangerment_Taxon.definition: Georgian is not considered endangered and is spoken by a large population. It is the official language of a sovereign state.
vitality_factors: Official status: Official language of the Republic of Georgia
Documentation: Extensive literature, textbooks, dictionaries, and media.
Literacy programs: Highly developed educational system in Georgian.

Language_Family.definition: Georgian is a member of the Kartvelian language family.

Language_Stock.definition: The Kartvelian language family is not considered part of any larger established stock, though it is sometimes included in hypothetical macro-families like Nostratic or Dene-Caucasian.

Language_Subfamily.definition: Georgian is the only member of its subfamily within Kartvelian; the others are Mingrelian-Laz (Zan) and Svan.

Isolate.definition: The Kartvelian family is an isolate family, not demonstrably related to any other language family.

Dialect.definition: Georgian has a number of regional dialects, classified into Eastern and Western groups.

dialects.name: Eastern Group
dialects.notes: Kartlian and Kakhetian form the basis of the standard language.

dialects.name: Western Group
dialects.notes: Imeretian and Gurian have distinct verb morphology and phonology.

dialects.name: Mountain Group
dialects.notes: Archaic features, unique vocabulary, and complex consonant clusters.

Dialect.standard_dialect: The literary standard is primarily based on the Kartlian dialect (Eastern group), with significant influence from Kakhetian and the literary tradition centered in Tbilisi.

The_Linguistic_Sign.definition: Georgian linguistic signs connect a signifier (phonological form) with a signified (meaning).

Signifier.definition: The external form, which can be spoken or written.
Signifier.details: Georgian uses the Mkhedruli script (33 letters). The spoken form is based on a system of 5 vowels and 28 consonant phonemes, with complex consonant clusters and ejective consonants.

Signified.details: Lexical meaning (e.g., სახლი saxli 'house', წიგნი cigni 'book', წერა cera 'writing') and grammatical meaning (e.g., plural -eb-, ergative -ma, past tense).

Arbitrariness.definition: Predominantly arbitrary, but with some onomatopoeic elements.
Arbitrariness.details: Most words are arbitrary, though some words like ბზუილი bzuili (buzzing) are onomatopoeic.

Linear_Character.definition: Elements follow one another in time.
Linear_Character.details: SOV word order; suffixes and prefixes are added linearly to roots.

Double_Articulation.definition: Signs are composed of smaller meaningful signs (morphemes) and non-meaningful units (phonemes).

The_Linguistic_Sign.examples: Words and morphemes: სახლი saxli 'house', -eb- (plural), წერ- cer- 'write', -თ -t (2PL subject marker).

Linguistic_Unit.definition: Linguistic units in Georgian are organized hierarchically.

Form_Unit.definition: The sensorily perceptible aspect of the sign, i.e., its spoken or written form.

Grammar_Unit.definition: The structural component of the sign, including morphemes and syntactic words.
examples: Syntactic words: სახლები saxlebi 'houses', დავწერე davc'ere 'I wrote'

Semantic_Unit.definition: The meaning component of the sign.

semantic_units.definition: სახლი saxli 'house', წერა cera 'to write', ლამაზი lamazi 'beautiful'.
Plural number (-eb-), ergative case (-ma), past tense (aorist screeve).

Linguistic_Expression.definition: The physical representation of a linguistic unit.

expressions.Spoken: The spoken form of Georgian, produced by the vocal apparatus.
expressions.Written: The written form, using the Mkhedruli script (33 letters, no capitals).

Spoken_Linguistic_Expression.definition: The physical sound form of Georgian, including dialectal variations and fast-speech processes.
Spoken_Linguistic_Expression.notes: Fast speech often involves the reduction of vowels and simplification of consonant clusters (e.g., სადა ხარ? sada xar? → სად ხარ? sad xar? 'Where are you?').

Written_Linguistic_Expression.definition: The written form of Georgian, using the Mkhedruli script (33 letters) adopted in the 5th century AD. The script is phonemic and has no capital letters.
Written_Linguistic_Expression.notes: The Mkhedruli script contains 5 vowels and 28 consonants. The written language is based on the Standard Georgian of the Republic.

Signed_Linguistic_Expression.definition: Not applicable. Georgian is primarily spoken and written; a signed variety exists (Georgian Sign Language) but is not a primary focus of this ontology.

Linguistic_Property.definition: Properties that characterize linguistic units in Georgian.

structures.definition: Dictionary entry: სახლი saxli 'house', სახლები saxlebi 'houses'.
Set of case forms for სახლი: სახლი (nom.), სახლის (gen.), სახლს (dat.), სახლით (instr.), სახლად (adv.), სახლო (voc.).

Literary_Language.definition: The standard, codified form of Georgian used in official contexts and education.

variants.Codified: Used in official and prepared communication, based on the Kartlian dialect.
variants.Spoken: Used in informal communication, may include colloquialisms.

Non-literary_Varieties.Social_Dialects: Differences between urban and rural varieties; age-based variations.
Non-literary_Varieties.Vernacular: Colloquial speech, often characterized by reduced forms and borrowing.

Thing.definition: In GOLD ontology, Thing is the superclass of all classes. All linguistic units are instances of Thing.

Abstract.definition: Grammatical categories in Georgian are abstract: number, tense, aspect, mood, case, version.

Object.definition: Georgian nouns refer to objects: სახლი saxli 'house' (physical object), კაცი k'ac'i 'man' (human), თბილისი Tbilisi 'city' (location).

Process.definition: Georgian verbs describe processes: წერა c'era 'to write', კითხვა k'itxva 'to read', სიარული siaruli 'to walk', ცხოვრება cxovreba 'to live'.

Phonetics.definition: The study of the sound system of Georgian, based primarily on the articulatory and acoustic properties of its consonants and vowels.

sub-branches.Articulatory: Study of how Georgian speech sounds are produced (e.g., ejective stops, uvular consonants, complex consonant clusters).
sub-branches.Acoustic: Study of acoustic properties of Georgian vowels and consonants (e.g., formants, VOT of ejectives vs. aspirated stops).
sub-branches.Perceptual: Study of how Georgian sounds are perceived (e.g., distinguishing ejective /p'/, /t'/, /k'/ from aspirated /p/, /t/, /k/ and voiced /b/, /d/, /g/).

Linguistic_Phonetics.definition: Studies the function of sound means in Georgian, focusing on phonemes.
Linguistic_Phonetics.details: Georgian has 28 consonant and 5 vowel phonemes. Key functional elements include the three-way laryngeal contrast (voiced, aspirated voiceless, ejective), complex consonant clusters, and the absence of phonemic vowel length.

Phonetic_Units.definition: Linear objects in the speech chain.

types.name: Sound
types.definition: Concrete realization of a phoneme in a specific context (e.g., aspirated [tʰ] in თბილისი [tʰbilisi] 'Tbilisi').

types.name: Sound Type
types.definition: Abstract grouping of phonetically similar sounds (e.g., all aspirated stops).

types.name: Phoneme
types.definition: Abstract unit that distinguishes meaning (e.g., /p/ vs /p'/ in პირი p'iri 'mouth' vs პირი piri 'elephant' - note: real minimal pair is ფარი pʰari 'shield' vs პარი p'ari 'pair' vs ბარი bari 'pen' - three-way contrast).

Suprasegmental_Units.definition: Units consisting of segmental units organized into larger prosodic structures.

Segment_Features: Place of articulation (labial, dental/alveolar, postalveolar, velar, uvular, glottal)
Manner of articulation (stop, affricate, fricative, nasal, liquid, glide)
Suprasegmental_Features: Stress (weak, dynamic, usually on the first syllable of a word; can shift with some suffixes)
Intonation (falling for statements, rising for yes/no questions, falling for wh-questions)

Phonetic_Rules.definition: Rules governing the use and variation of phonetic units.
Phonological_Rules: Consonant clusters: Georgian allows up to six consonants initially (e.g., ბრძოლა brdzola 'fight'). No vowel epenthesis occurs.
Voicing assimilation: Some assimilation occurs in clusters, but is not fully systematic.
Ejective neutralization: Ejectives may lose glottalization in fast speech or word-final position.
Vowel reduction: In fast speech, unstressed vowels may be reduced or elided.
Final devoicing: Voiced stops /b, d, g/ may be partially devoiced word-finally, but not completely.
Coarticulatory_Rules: Palatalization of velars before front vowels.
Labialization of consonants before rounded vowels.
Nasalization of vowels adjacent to nasal consonants.

Consonants.definition: 28 consonant phonemes in Georgian, with a three-way laryngeal contrast for stops and affricates.

Uvular.notes: Often accompanied by strong friction; no voiced or aspirated counterpart.

phonological_notes.three_way_contrast: The three-way laryngeal contrast (voiced, aspirated, ejective) for stops and affricates is a key feature of Georgian.
phonological_notes.ejectives: Ejective (glottalized) consonants are produced with a simultaneous glottal closure and oral closure, releasing with a sharp pop.
phonological_notes.uvular_q: ყ q' is a uvular ejective with strong friction; learners often struggle with its pronunciation.
phonological_notes.v_allophony: ვ v has multiple allophones: [v] before vowels, [w] after vowels, [ʋ] in some contexts.
phonological_notes.r_allophony: რ r is typically a tap [ɾ], but can be a trill [r] in emphatic speech.
phonological_notes.l_allophony: ლ l has a velarized allophone [ɫ] in some positions and a palatalized allophone [lʲ] before front vowels.

minimal_pairs.pair: ფარი pʰari 'shield' vs პარი p'ari 'pair' vs ბარი bari 'pen'
თაგვი tʰagvi 'mouse' vs ტაგვი t'agvi (not a word) vs დაგვი dagvi (not a word)
ქარი kʰari 'wind' vs კარი k'ari 'door' vs გარი gari (not a word)
ცა tsʰa 'sky' vs წა ts'a (not a word) vs ძა dza (not a word)
ჩაი tʃʰai 'tea' vs ჭაი tʃ'ai (not a word) vs ჯაი dʒai (not a word)
სალი sali 'hall' vs ზალი zali (not a word)
შარი ʃari 'arrow' vs ჟარი ʒari (not a word)

Vowels.definition: 5 vowel phonemes in Georgian, with no phonemic length distinction.
Vowels.vowel_harmony: Georgian does not have vowel harmony. Vowels can occur freely in any position.

minimal_pairs.pair: და da 'and' vs დე de (not a word)
სი si (not a word) vs სუ su (not a word)
კო ko (not a word) vs კა ka (not a word)

length_contrast.definition: Vowel length is not phonemic in Georgian. Long vowels may occur in loanwords or as a result of consonant elision, but they do not create minimal pairs.

Syllable.definition: In Georgian, syllables follow a structure of (C)(C)(C)(C)(C)(C)V(C)(C)(C)(C)(C)(C).

structures.V: Rare; occurs in some pronouns and conjunctions (e.g., ა a 'or').
structures.CV: Very frequent (e.g., ბა ba, და da).

Stress.definition: Stress in Georgian is weak and dynamic, usually on the first syllable of a word. Adding suffixes can shift stress to the new first syllable.
exceptions: Some words have stress on other syllables, especially in loanwords or compound words.
In some dialects (e.g., Imeretian), stress patterns differ.

Intonation.definition: Intonation is used to distinguish sentence types.
functions: Rising intonation for yes/no questions (in colloquial speech).

Consonant_Clusters.definition: Georgian is famous for its complex consonant clusters, allowing up to six consonants initially and up to four finally.
Consonant_Clusters.notes: No vowel epenthesis occurs in these clusters; speakers articulate them fluently. This is a major challenge for learners.

Ejective_Consonants.definition: Ejective (glottalized) consonants are a hallmark of Georgian phonology. They are produced with a simultaneous glottal closure and oral closure, releasing with a sharp pop.
Ejective_Consonants.notes: Learners must distinguish ejectives from aspirated and voiced counterparts. For example, პარი p'ari 'pair' vs ფარი pʰari 'shield' vs ბარი bari 'pen'.

Vowel_System.definition: Georgian has 5 vowel phonemes with no length distinction.
Vowel_System.notes: Vowels are pronounced clearly and without reduction in careful speech. In fast speech, unstressed vowels may be reduced or elided.

Phonological_System.definition: The phonological system of Georgian is based on a system of 5 vowels and 28 consonants, with a three-way laryngeal contrast, complex consonant clusters, and no phonemic vowel length or stress.
Phonological_System.vowel_system: 5 vowels: ა a, ე e, ი i, ო o, უ u. No length distinction.
Phonological_System.consonant_system: 28 consonants with contrasts in voicing (voiced, aspirated voiceless, ejective), place, and manner.

Orthographic_System.definition: Georgian has a standardized orthography based on the Mkhedruli script, which has been in use since the 5th century AD.
Orthographic_System.alphabet: 33 letters: ა a, ბ b, გ g, დ d, ე e, ვ v, ზ z, თ t, ი i, კ k', ლ l, მ m, ნ n, ო o, პ p', ჟ ʒ, რ r, ს s, ტ t', უ u, ფ p, ქ k, ღ ɣ, ყ q', შ ʃ, ჩ tʃ, ც ts, ძ dz, წ ts', ჭ tʃ', ხ x, ჯ dʒ, ჰ h.

vowel_representation.oral: ა a, ე e, ი i, ო o, უ u
vowel_representation.notes: Vowels are represented by distinct letters. No length marking.

consonant_representation.notes: Distinct letters for ejectives (პ, ტ, კ, ყ, წ, ჭ) and their aspirated and voiced counterparts (ფ, თ, ქ, ც, ჩ; ბ, დ, გ, ძ, ჯ).

tonal_marking.notes: Georgian is not a tonal language. Stress is not marked orthographically.

Orthographic_System.punctuation: Uses standard Western punctuation marks (.,!?, etc.).

Morphology.definition: The branch of linguistics studying the internal structure of words in Georgian. Georgian is an agglutinative-fusional language with rich prefixation and suffixation, poly-personal verb agreement, split ergativity, and a highly complex system of screeves (tense-aspect-mood paradigms).
Morphology.key_focus: Identifying patterns of systematic covariation between form and meaning, particularly in poly-personal agreement, version, preverbation, and ergative case marking.

Goals.elegant_description: Capture generalizations about Georgian morphology, especially its poly-personal agreement and version system.
Goals.cognitively_realistic_description: Reflect the mental grammar of Georgian speakers, including the distinction between Series I, II, and III screeves.
Goals.system_external_explanation: Link morphological patterns to factors outside the system, such as historical contact with Iranian, Arabic, Turkish, and Russian languages.

Word.definition: A complex concept with several distinct senses in Georgian.

Lexeme.definition: An abstract dictionary word representing a core meaning.
types: Simple: სახლი saxli 'house', წიგნი c'igni 'book', წერა c'era 'to write'
Compound: მთისწვერი mtisc'veri 'mountain peak' (mta 'mountain' + c'veri 'peak'), წყალსაცავი c'q'alsacavi 'reservoir' (c'q'ali 'water' + sacavi 'container')

Word-form.definition: A concrete occurrence of a lexeme in speech.

Word_token.definition: A specific occurrence in a text.
Word_token.example: The token სახლი in the sentence 'ეს სახლია' es saxl-ia 'This is a house'

Morpheme.definition: The smallest meaningful (sign) unit in Georgian. Cannot be divided into smaller meaningful parts.
Morpheme.key_properties: Cannot be divided into smaller meaningful parts.

Free.definition: Can stand alone as a word.

Bound.definition: Cannot stand alone, must attach to another morpheme.

Cumulation.definition: Expression of multiple meanings by a single marker.
types: Grammatical: The suffix -ა -a in არის aris 'is' marks both 3SG subject and present tense.
Grammatical: The suffix -თ -t marks both 2PL subject and plurality of the direct object in some forms.
Lexical and Grammatical: The prefix მ- m- in მწერალი mc'erali 'writer' marks both agentive and the lexical root c'er-.

Allomorphy.definition: Variation in form of a morpheme.
conditioning: Phonological: The plural suffix has allomorphs -ებ- -eb- and -ნ- -n- depending on the root.
Grammatical: The 1SG subject prefix has allomorphs ვ- v- and ვ- - -თ -t depending on screeve.
Lexical: Some roots have suppletive forms (e.g., მიდის midis 'goes' vs წავიდა c'avida 'went').

deviations_from_additive_model.Fusion: Loss of clear boundary between morphemes in some contracted forms (e.g., მაქვს makvs 'I have' contains fused agreement markers).

types_by_expression.Operational: Modification of another morpheme: vowel syncope in some roots (e.g., ქვეყანა kveq'ana 'country' → ქვეყნის kveq'nis 'of the country').
types_by_expression.Zero: Meaningful absence: nominative case has zero suffix (e.g., სახლი saxli 'house' vs სახლმა saxlma 'house (ERG)').

Morph.definition: A concrete, linear realization of a morpheme.

examples.-ებ- -eb-: allomorph of plural suffix after most roots (e.g., სახლები saxlebi 'houses')
examples.-ნ- -n-: allomorph of plural suffix after some roots (e.g., ქვეყნები kveq'nebi 'countries')

Affix.definition: A bound morpheme attaching to a base. Georgian uses both prefixes and suffixes, though suffixation is more common.

examples: ა- a- (version vowel, e.g., აკეთებs ak'etebs 'he does it')
ი- i- (version vowel, e.g., იწერს ic'ers 'he writes to himself')
უ- u- (version vowel, e.g., უწერს uc'ers 'he writes to him')

Suffix.definition: Attach to end of root. This is the primary morphological device in Georgian.

Circumfix.definition: Discontinuous affix that occurs on both sides of the base.
examples: ა- -ებ- a- -eb- (causative, e.g., აკეთებს ak'etebs 'he makes someone do')

Root.definition: The base form of a word which cannot be further analyzed without total loss of identity.

examples.free: სახლი saxli 'house', წიგნი c'igni 'book', წყალი c'q'ali 'water'
examples.bound: წერ- c'er- (in მწერალი mc'erali 'writer'), კითხ- k'itx- (in მკითხველი mk'itxveli 'reader')

Stem.definition: A root plus one or more derivational suffixes, to which inflectional suffixes are added.

Syncope.definition: Loss of a vowel in the root in certain morphological contexts.

Clitic.definition: A prosodically dependent unit with syntactic freedom.

Proclitic.definition: A clitic that precedes the lexical unit.
examples: ვერ ver 'cannot' (e.g., ვერ მოვდივარ ver movdivar 'I cannot come')

Enclitic.definition: A clitic that is phonologically joined at the end.

Compound.definition: A linguistic unit composed of elements that function independently.
Compound.structure: Two or more words combined; plural marked on the second element.

examples.Noun+Noun (genitive): სახლის კარი saxis k'ari 'house door' (saxli 'house' + k'ari 'door')
examples.Adjective+Noun: შავთვალა ქალი šavtvala kali 'black-eyed woman' (šavi 'black' + tvali 'eye')

types.Endocentric: The compound is a hyponym of its head: მთისწვერი (a type of c'veri 'peak')
types.Exocentric: The meaning is not derived from the parts: ცხრაფეხა cxrapexa 'spider' (cxra 'nine' + pexi 'foot')

Inflection.definition: Morphological relationship between word-forms of a single lexeme.
categories: Case (7 cases: nominative, ergative, dative, genitive, instrumental, adverbial, vocative)

key_properties: Less regular and productive than inflection

-ელ- -el-.function: Forms agent nouns and adjectives from nouns or verbs

-ობ- -ob-.function: Forms abstract nouns from adjectives and nouns

-ებ- -eb-.function: Forms abstract nouns from adjectives and verbs

-იან- -ian-.function: Forms adjectives from nouns meaning 'having, with'

-ურ- -ur-.function: Forms adjectives from nouns meaning 'related to, of'

სა- sa-.function: Forms future participles and nouns of purpose/place

Compounding.definition: Combination of two or more lexemes to form a new one.

types.Endocentric: One element is the head: მთისწვერი mtisc'veri 'mountain peak' (c'veri 'peak' is the head)
types.Exocentric: No clear head: ცხრაფეხა cxrapexa 'spider' (cxra 'nine' + pexi 'foot')

examples.Noun+Noun: მთისწვერი mtisc'veri 'mountain peak', წყალსაცავი c'q'alsacavi 'reservoir', სახლის კარი saxis k'ari 'house door'

Morphological_Operations.Word_Formation: Cover term for derivation and compounding.

Lexicon.definition: The total store of words available to a speaker. Georgian lexicon contains native Kartvelian roots and extensive borrowings from Iranian, Arabic, Turkish, Russian, and European languages.
Lexicon.notes: Georgian lexicon includes nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, postpositions, particles, numerals, and ideophones.

Lexical_Item.definition: A unit of the vocabulary. Includes native Kartvelian roots and numerous borrowings.

Inflectional_Paradigm.definition: The complete set of grammatical word-forms of a lexeme.
Inflectional_Paradigm.Inflection_Class: Group of lexemes sharing the same set of forms. Georgian has regular and irregular paradigms.
Inflectional_Paradigm.Syncretism: Two or more functions expressed by the same form (e.g., -ს -s marks both dative and genitive in some paradigms).
Inflectional_Paradigm.Periphrasis: Use of a separate word or phrase (e.g., future tense in some verbs uses a particle).

Grammatical_Meaning.definition: Meanings obligatorily expressed by the grammar.
Grammatical_Meaning.Grammatical_Category: A set of mutually exclusive, obligatory meanings.
Grammatical_Meaning.Grammeme: An individual value within a category.

Agreement_Class_Gender.definition: Georgian does not have grammatical gender. Natural gender is expressed lexically (e.g., კაცი k'ac'i 'man' vs ქალი kali 'woman') or through distinct words (e.g., ძმა dzma 'brother' vs და da 'sister').

Case.definition: Marks syntactic and/or semantic role through suffixes. There are seven cases in Georgian.

Nominative.function: Subject of intransitive verbs, direct object in Series I, subject in Series III

Ergative.function: Subject of transitive verbs in Series II (aorist)

Dative.function: Indirect object, direct object in Series I and II, subject of indirect verbs

plural_suffix.rule: The plural marker precedes the case marker.

special_cases.pluralia_tantum: Words with only plural form: შარვალი šarvali 'trousers', სათვალე satvale 'glasses'
special_cases.mass_nouns: Do not take plural when used generically: წყალი c'q'ali 'water', ღვინო ɣvino 'wine'

referential_usage.Definite: Marked by zero (definite meaning is implied), or by word order and context
referential_usage.Indefinite: Marked by ვინმე vinme 'someone' or რაღაც raɣac 'something', or by zero

non-referential_usage.Generic: Unmarked noun: ადამიანი მოკვდავია adamiani mok'vdavia 'Man is mortal.'

Possession.definition: Possession is expressed through possessive pronouns and suffixes on the possessed noun.

Aspect.definition: Presents situation from internal temporal perspective.

core_meanings.Perfective: Action viewed as a whole (aorist, perfect)
core_meanings.Imperfective: Action viewed as ongoing (present, imperfect, present subjunctive)

Tense.definition: Locates event relative to moment of speech.

Present_Indicative.example: ვწერ vc'er 'I write', წერ c'er 'you write', წერს c'ers 'he writes', წერენ c'eren 'they write'

Future_Indicative.example: დავწერ davc'er 'I will write', დაწერ dac'er 'you will write', დაწერს dac'ers 'he will write'

Aorist.example: დავწერე davc'ere 'I wrote', დაწერე dac'ere 'you wrote', დაწერა dac'era 'he wrote', დაწერეს dac'eres 'they wrote'

Imperfect.example: ვწერდი vc'erdi 'I was writing', წერდი c'erdi 'you were writing', წერდა c'erda 'he was writing', წერდნენ c'erdnen 'they were writing'

Perfect.example: დამიწერია damic'eria 'I have apparently written', დაგიწერია dagic'eria 'you have apparently written', დაუწერია dauc'eria 'he has apparently written', დაუწერიათ dauc'eriat 'they have apparently written'

Pluperfect.example: დამეწერა damec'era 'I had written', დაგეწერა dagec'era 'you had written', დაეწერა daec'era 'he had written', დაეწერათ daec'erat 'they had written'

negation_suffix.example: არ დავწერე ar davc'ere 'I didn't write' (I refused to write), ვერ დავწერე ver davc'ere 'I couldn't write'

Subjunctive.example: დავწერო davc'ero 'that I may write', დავწერა davc'era 'that I may be writing', დავწერე davc'ere 'if I were to write'

Conditional.example: დავწერდი davc'erdi 'I would write', დაწერდი dac'erdi 'you would write', დაწერდა dac'erda 'he would write', დაწერდნენ dac'erdnen 'they would write'

subtypes.Active: Default voice. The subject performs the action.

Passive.rule: In Series I, passive verbs take nominative subject and dative indirect object.

Causative.example: აკეთებინებს ak'etebinebs 'he makes someone do it'
Causative.rule: Causative verbs add an agent (causer) to the argument structure.

Reflexive.rule: Reflexive verbs indicate the subject acts upon itself.

Reciprocal.example: იწერებიან ic'erebian 'they write to each other'
Reciprocal.rule: Reciprocal verbs indicate a mutual action.

Version.definition: A grammatical category unique to Kartvelian languages that indicates the relationship between the verb and its indirect object.

Subjective.definition: Action for oneself or on one's own behalf
Subjective.example: იკეთებს ik'etebs 'he does it for himself'

Objective.example: უკეთებს uk'etebs 'he does it for him'

Locative.example: აკეთებს ak'etebs 'he does it on it' (rare)

Version.notes: Version is a hallmark of Georgian morphology. It interacts with the screeve system and case marking.

Screeves.definition: The Georgian tense-aspect-mood system consists of 11 screeves (from the Greek 'skhēma' via Latin 'schema'), organized into three series.

Series_I.description: Present sub-series: subject in nominative, direct object in dative.

Series_II.description: Aorist sub-series: subject in ergative (transitive), direct object in nominative.

Series_III.description: Perfect sub-series: subject in dative, direct object in nominative.

Inflection_vs_Derivation_Criteria: Relevance to syntax: Inflection is more relevant (case, agreement)
Obligatoriness: Inflection is more obligatory (case, tense)
Regularity and productivity: Inflection is more regular
Meaning compositionality: Inflection is more compositional
Word class change: Derivation can change class
Position relative to base: Derivation is closer to root

processes: Vowel syncope in noun declension (e.g., ქვეყანა kveq'ana 'country' → ქვეყნის kveq'nis 'of the country')
Consonant alternations (e.g., t→d, k→g, q→x in some contexts)
Elision of final vowels before suffixes

Syntax-Morphology_Interface.lexical_integrity: Syntactic rules cannot access internal morphological structure.

Morphology_and_Other_Components.Morphology_and_Valence: How morphology affects argument structure: causative adds an agent, passive removes an agent, reciprocal adds a plural subject.

Productivity.definition: Ability to apply to new bases.
restrictions: Phonological: Some suffixes are sensitive to vowel harmony or syncope
Semantic: Some derivational suffixes only apply to certain semantic classes
Pragmatic: Some strategies are less productive
Morphological: Borrowed vocabulary may not take all suffixes
Productivity.blocking: Existing word prevents formation of synonym

key_patterns: High frequency forms are irregular (e.g., ყოფნა qopna 'to be' has suppletive forms)

Morphological_Typology.Degree_of_Synthesis: High morpheme-per-word ratio; complex suffixation and prefixation

Part_Of_Speech_Property.definition: The property that identifies the grammatical class of a word.

classes.Noun: Names of entities; take plural, case, and possessive markers
classes.Verb: Actions and states; show TAM and agreement
classes.Adjective: Quality words; can be used as nouns
classes.Adverb: Modify verbs; often derived from adjectives with -ად -ad
classes.Postposition: Follow nouns; mark spatial, instrumental, and beneficiary relations

Bound_Morpheme.examples: Plural suffix -ებ- -eb-, ergative -მა -ma, genitive -ის -is, 1SG subject prefix ვ- v-

Free_Morpheme.examples: სახლი saxli 'house', წიგნი c'igni 'book', კაცი k'ac'i 'man'

Inflectional_Morpheme.definition: Express grammatical categories; do not change word class.
Inflectional_Morpheme.examples: Plural suffix -ებ- -eb-, case suffixes, tense suffixes, person agreement affixes

Derivational_Morpheme.definition: Derive new lexical units; may change word class.

Prefix.examples: ვ- v- (1SG), მ- m- (agentive), სა- sa- (future/place), ა- a- (version), ი- i- (version), უ- u- (version/privative)

Suffix.examples: All primary inflectional and derivational morphemes

Circumfix.definition: Discontinuous affix that occurs on both sides of the base.
Circumfix.examples: ა- -ებ- a- -eb- (causative), სა- -ე sa- -e (place), უ- -ო u- -o (privative)

Category_Changer.definition: Derivational units that change the syntactic category of the root.

Nominalizer.definition: Forms a noun from some other word class.

Copula.definition: Indicates a relationship of equivalency between subject and predicate.
Copula.examples: არის aris 'is', არიან arian 'are', ვარ var 'I am', ხარ xar 'you are', ვართ vart 'we are', ხართ xart 'you (PL) are'

Auxiliary.definition: Verbs used in coordination with another verb to express mood, tense or aspect.
Auxiliary.examples: შეიძლება šeidzleba 'it is possible' (for potential), უნდა unda 'must' (for obligation)

Negation_Operator.examples: არ ar (simple negation), ვერ ver (inability), ნუ nu (prohibition)

Pro_Form.examples: ვინ vin 'who', რა ra 'what', რომელი romeli 'which'

Personal_Pronoun.definition: Refers to speaker, addressee, and others.

Demonstrative.definition: Used deictically to indicate spatial, temporal, or discourse location.

examples.plural: ესენი eseni 'these', ეგენი egeni 'those (near you)', ისინი isini 'those (over there)'

Quantifier.definition: Expresses definite or indefinite number or amount.

Voice_Values.Causative: Marked by circumfix ა- -ებ- a- -eb- or -ინ- -in-

Case_Property.definition: Grammatical encoding of a noun's relationship to other elements.
Case_Property.examples: Nominative (-ი -i or zero), Ergative (-მა -ma), Dative (-ს -s), Genitive (-ის -is), Instrumental (-ით -it), Adverbial (-ად -ad), Vocative (-ო -o)

Modality_Property.examples: Epistemic (ალბათ albat 'probably'), Deontic (უნდა unda 'must', შეიძლება šeidzleba 'may')

Evidentiality_Property.definition: Basis for claiming event has occurred.
Evidentiality_Property.examples: Direct (unmarked), Indirect (Perfect screeve with -ი-ა -i-a), Reported (ამბობენ amboben 'they say')

Generative_Grammar.definition: Grammar viewed as a cognitive faculty; language generated by a set of rules.

key_assumptions.I-Language: Internal, psychological, cognitive system of grammatical knowledge
key_assumptions.E-Language: External, physical, social manifestation of language
key_assumptions.Performance: Actual use of language, subject to external factors

Basic_Word_Order.definition: SOV (Subject-Object-Verb) order is the basic, unmarked order in Georgian. However, word order is pragmatically flexible, allowing for topicalization and focus.
Basic_Word_Order.example: მე წიგნს ვკითხულობ. me c'igns vk'itxulob. 'I am reading a book.'

variations.OSV: For emphasis: წიგნს მე ვკითხულობ. c'igns me vk'itxulob. 'It's me who is reading the book.'
variations.SVO: Less common, but possible in some contexts: მე ვკითხულობ წიგნს. me vk'itxulob c'igns. 'I am reading a book.'
variations.VSO: Rare, in some questions: ვკითხულობ მე წიგნს? vk'itxulob me c'igns? 'Am I reading a book?'

Postpositions.definition: Function words that follow nouns to indicate case relations. Georgian uses postpositions rather than prepositions.

examples.ზე ze: on, about (e.g., მაგიდაზე magidaze 'on the table')
examples.ში ši: in, into (e.g., სახლში saxliš 'in the house')
examples.მდე mde: up to, until (e.g., სახლამდე saxlamde 'up to the house')
examples.თან tan: at, by (e.g., მეგობართან megobartan 'at a friend's place')
examples.შორის šoris: among, between (e.g., ხეებს შორის xebs šoris 'among the trees')
examples.გარეშე gareshe: without (e.g., შენ გარეშე šen gareshe 'without you')
examples.გამო gamo: because of (e.g., ამის გამო amis gamo 'because of this')
examples.მიხედვით mix-edvit: according to (e.g., კანონის მიხედვით k'anonis mixedvit 'according to the law')

examples.negative: არ დავწერე ar davc'ere 'I didn't write (I refused to)'
ვერ დავწერე ver davc'ere 'I couldn't write'

nominal_negation.example: ეს არ არის სახლი. es ar aris saxli. 'This is not a house.'

existential_negation.example: ფული არ მაქვს. puli ar makvs. 'I don't have money.'

yes_no.example: წიგნს კითხულობ? c'igns k'itxulob? 'Are you reading a book?'
yes_no.alternative: Question particle -ა -a attached to the focused word: წიგნსა კითხულობ? c'ignsa k'itxulob?

wh.example: ეს რა არის? es ra aris? 'What is this?'
wh.word_order: The interrogative word typically immediately precedes the verb.

Theta_Roles.Theta_Criterion: Each argument assigned one and only one theta role; each theta role assigned to one argument.

Constituents.definition: A group of words functioning as a single unit.

examples.phrase: ორი დიდი სახლი ori didi saxli 'two big houses'
დიდ სახლში did saxliš 'in the big house'

Verb_Phrase.structure: (Preverb) (Version) (Subject Agreement) Root (Thematic Suffix) (Tense Suffix) (Object Agreement) (Plural Suffix)

examples.phrase: წიგნს ვკითხულობ c'igns vk'itxulob 'I am reading a book'
სწრაფად ვკითხულობ sc'rapad vk'itxulob 'I read quickly'
წიგნს დავწერ c'igns davc'er 'I will write a book'

examples: სახლზე დიდი saxlze didi 'bigger than the house'

Clause_Structure.example: მე წიგნს ვკითხულობ. me c'igns vk'itxulob. 'I am reading a book.'

Interrogative.content: შენ რომელ წიგნს კითხულობ? šen romel c'igns k'itxulob? 'Which book are you reading?'

Imperative.singular: წიგნი იკითხე! c'igni ik'itxe! 'Read the book!'
Imperative.plural: წიგნი იკითხეთ! c'igni ik'itxet! 'Read the book (PL)!'
Imperative.prohibition: წიგნი ნუ იკითხავ! c'igni nu ik'itxav! 'Don't read the book!'

Conditional.example: თუ მოხვალ, მეც მოვალ. tu moxval, mec moval. 'If you come, I will come too.'

examples.clause: მოსული კაცი mosuli k'ac'i 'the man who has come'
წიგნის კითხვა c'ignis k'itxva 'reading a book'

Nominal_Clause.example: მე ვიცი, რომ ის მოვა. me vici, rom is mova. 'I know that he will come.'

Theme_and_Rheme.Theme: Starting point, what sentence is about.
Theme_and_Rheme.Rheme: New information, what is said about theme.

Communicative_Categories.Topic: Grammaticalized theme, often marked by position at the beginning of sentence.
Communicative_Categories.Focus: Most salient, emphasized part; often fronted immediately before the verb.
Communicative_Categories.Given_vs_New: Information assumed known vs. newly introduced.

Agreement.definition: Poly-personal agreement in Georgian: the verb agrees with the subject, direct object, and indirect object through affixes.
Agreement.example: მე შენ წიგნს გაძლევ. me šen c'igns gadzlev. 'I give you a book.' (გ- g- marks 2SG indirect object, -ძლევ -dzlev is the root)

Government.definition: Postpositions and verbs determine case marking of noun phrases.

Adjunct.definition: A phrase modifying a head but not an actant.

Syntactic_Relations.Apposition: Two noun phrases juxtaposed referring to the same entity.
Syntactic_Relations.example: ნადირი, ჩემი მეგობარი, აქ ცხოვრობს. nadiri, č'emi megobari, ak cxovrobs. 'Nadiri, my friend, lives here.'

Screeves_System.definition: The Georgian verb system is organized into three series of screeves (tense-aspect-mood paradigms), each with its own case-marking pattern.

Series_I.description: Present sub-series: Nominative subject, Dative direct object for transitives.
Series_I.example: მე წიგნს ვწერ. me c'igns vc'er. 'I am writing a book.'

Series_II.description: Aorist sub-series: Ergative subject, Nominative direct object for transitives.
Series_II.example: მე წიგნი დავწერე. me c'igni davc'ere. 'I wrote a book.'

Series_III.description: Perfect sub-series: Dative subject, Nominative direct object for transitives (inverted syntax).
Series_III.example: მე წიგნი დამიწერია. me c'igni damic'eria. 'I have apparently written a book.'

Ergativity.definition: Georgian displays split ergativity: the ergative case is used for the subject of transitive verbs in Series II (aorist).
Ergativity.example: კაცმა წიგნი დაწერა. k'ac'ma c'igni dac'era. 'The man wrote a book.' (k'ac'ma = man-ERG)

Poly_Personal_Agreement.definition: The Georgian verb agrees with up to three arguments: subject, direct object, and indirect object.
Poly_Personal_Agreement.example: მე შენ წიგნს გაძლევ. me šen c'igns gadzlev. 'I give you a book.'

Preverbs.definition: Preverbs are prefixes that indicate direction and aspect. They are essential for forming future and aorist screeves.

Version.definition: Version is a grammatical category that indicates the relationship between the verb and its indirect object.

types.Neutral: No specific indirect object relationship (vowel: ა- a-)
types.Objective: Action for someone else (vowel: უ- u-)

Coordination.definition: Clauses of equal status joined by conjunctions.
Coordination.example: მე ვკითხულობ და ის წერს. me vk'itxulob da is c'ers. 'I read and he writes.'

Subordination.definition: Clauses of unequal status, with one clause (subordinate) dependent on another (main).
types: Complement clauses: introduced by რომ rom 'that'
Relative clauses: introduced by participles or რომელი romeli 'which'
Adverbial clauses: introduced by conjunctions like თუ tu 'if', როცა roc'a 'when', სანამ sanam 'until', რადგან radgan 'because'

examples.example: მე ვიცი, რომ ის მოვა. me vici, rom is mova. 'I know that he will come.'
თუ მოხვალ, მეც მოვალ. tu moxval, mec moval. 'If you come, I will come too.'
როცა ის მოვიდა, მე ვწერდი. roc'a is movida, me vc'erdi. 'When he came, I was writing.'
რადგან წვიმდა, სახლში დავრჩი. radgan c'vimda, saxlši davrč'i. 'Because it was raining, I stayed at home.'

Word_Order_Flexibility.definition: Georgian word order is pragmatically flexible, allowing for topicalization and focus.

examples.neutral: მე წიგნს ვკითხულობ. me c'igns vk'itxulob. 'I am reading a book.'

examples.topic_fronted: წიგნს მე ვკითხულობ. c'igns me vk'itxulob. 'The book, I am reading (it).'

examples.focus_fronted: მე წიგნს ვკითხულობ. me c'igns vk'itxulob. (with emphasis on 'I')

Null_Subjects.definition: Subject pronouns are often omitted because the verb already marks person and number.
Null_Subjects.example: ვკითხულობ. vk'itxulob. 'I am reading.' (Subject 'me' is omitted)

Reflexivization.definition: Reflexive pronouns (თავი tavi 'self') are used for reflexive actions.
Reflexivization.example: ის თავს იბანს. is tavs ibans. 'He washes himself.'

Reciprocal.definition: Reciprocal actions are expressed with the prefix ი- i- and the suffix -ებ- -eb-.
Reciprocal.example: ისინი ერთმანეთს წერენ. isini ertmanets c'eren. 'They write to each other.'

Semantics.definition: The branch of linguistics studying meaning in Georgian.

Truth-Conditional_Semantics.definition: To know meaning is to know truth-conditions.

Compositionality.definition: Meaning of complex expression determined by meanings of parts and combination rules.

The_Linguistic_Sign.definition: Conventional relation between form and content.

complex_types.<a, b>: Functions from type a to type b

Lexicon_and_Interpretation.Lexicon: Specifies denotation for each lexical item.

Lexical_Meaning.definition: Meaning of a word as a unit of the lexicon.

components.Pragmatic_Component: Conditions of use and speaker's attitude

Synonymy: ლამაზი lamazi, მშვენიერი mšvenieri, კარგი k'argi 'beautiful, good'

Polysemy.definition: Single word with multiple related meanings.
Polysemy.example: თვალი tvali 'eye' also means 'source, spring' (თვალის წყარო tvalis c'q'aro 'spring water')

Grammatical_Meaning.definition: Abstract, obligatory, systematic meaning expressed by grammatical markers.
key_categories: Case (7 cases: nominative, ergative, dative, genitive, instrumental, adverbial, vocative)
Tense (present, future, aorist, imperfect, perfect, pluperfect)

Propositional_Component.Proposition: Set of possible worlds or truth-value.
Propositional_Component.Argument_Structure: List of participants with semantic roles.

Communicative_Component.Given_New: Information assumed known vs. newly introduced.

Pragmatic_Component.definition: Information about speaker's intention and use.
Pragmatic_Component.Illocutionary_Force: Type of act (assertion, question, command, wish)

Referential_Status.Definite: Implied by context or marked by word order: წიგნი c'igni 'the book'
Referential_Status.Indefinite: Marked by ვინმე vinme 'someone' or რაღაც raɣac 'something': რაღაც წიგნი raɣac c'igni 'some book'
Referential_Status.Generic: Unmarked: წიგნი სასარგებლოა. c'igni sasargebloa. 'Books are useful.'

Binding.conditions: Binder must c-command variable and share an index.

Binding_and_Anaphora.Binding_Principles: Syntactic constraints on anaphoric relations (Principles A, B, C).

Semantic_Metalanguages.definition: Formal languages used to describe meaning.

Phonetics-Phonology_Interface.definition: The interaction between the substance of speech (phonetics) and its functional organization in the linguistic system (phonology).

key_areas.name: Allophonic variation
examples: Aspirated stops [pʰ, tʰ, kʰ] occur in free variation with their unaspirated counterparts in some contexts.
Ejectives [p', t', k', q'] may lose glottalization in fast speech or word-final position.
Voiced stops [b, d, g] may be partially devoiced word-finally, but remain distinct from voiceless stops.

key_areas.name: Phonological rules
examples: Consonant clusters: Georgian allows up to six consonants initially (e.g., მწვრთნელი mts'vrtneli 'trainer').
No vowel epenthesis occurs in clusters.
Palatalization of velars before front vowels: კ k' → კ' k'ʲ before ი i, ე e.
Labialization of consonants before rounded vowels: შ š → შʷ before უ u, ო o.

key_areas.name: Phonetic transcription
examples: Mapping from phonemes to phonetic realization: /p/ → [pʰ] initially, [p] in clusters.

Phonology-Morphology_Interface.definition: The interaction between sound structure and word structure.

key_areas.name: Morphophonology
examples: Vowel syncope: ქვეყანა kveq'ana 'country' → ქვეყნის kveq'nis 'of the country'.
Consonant alternations: t → d in some verb forms (e.g., წერს c'ers 'writes' → დაწერა dac'era 'wrote').
Elision of final vowels before suffixes: სახლი saxli 'house' → სახლს saxls 'house (DAT)'.
Compensatory lengthening: when a consonant is lost, the preceding vowel may lengthen.

key_areas.name: Allomorphy
examples: Plural suffix allomorphs: -ებ- -eb- (most roots) vs -ნ- -n- (some roots).
1SG subject prefix allomorphs: ვ- v- (present) vs ვ- - -თ -t (some screeves).
Case suffix allomorphs: -ს -s (dative) vs -ის -is (genitive) depending on the stem.

key_areas.name: Phonologically conditioned morphological rules
examples: The choice between -ებ- -eb- and -ნ- -n- plural suffixes is phonologically conditioned.
The epenthetic vowel -ა- -a- is inserted between some consonant clusters (e.g., ვწერ vc'er 'I write' vs ვწერე vc'ere 'I wrote').

Morphology-Syntax_Interface.definition: The interaction between word structure and sentence structure.

key_areas.name: Lexical Integrity
examples: Syntactic rules cannot access internal morphological structure.
The verb form is a single syntactic word, even though it contains many morphemes (e.g., დაგიწერია dagic'eria 'you have apparently written it to him').

key_areas.name: Agreement
examples: Poly-personal agreement: the verb agrees with subject, direct object, and indirect object through affixes.
Example: მე შენ წიგნს გაძლევ. me šen c'igns gadzlev. 'I give you a book.' (გ- g- marks 2SG indirect object)

key_areas.name: Case assignment
examples: Nominative case: subject of intransitive verbs and direct object in Series I.
Ergative case: subject of transitive verbs in Series II (aorist).
Dative case: indirect object and subject of indirect verbs.
Example: კაცმა წიგნი დაწერა. k'ac'ma c'igni dac'era. 'The man wrote a book.' (k'ac'ma = man-ERG, c'igni = book-NOM)

key_areas.name: Valence changing operations
examples: Causative adds an agent: აკეთებს ak'etebs 'he does it' → აკეთებინებს ak'etebinebs 'he makes someone do it'.
Passive removes an agent: წერს c'ers 'he writes' → იწერება ic'ereba 'it is written'.
Reciprocal: იწერებიან ic'erebian 'they write to each other'.

Syntax-Semantics_Interface.definition: The interaction between sentence structure and meaning.

key_areas.name: Compositionality
examples: Meaning derived from parts and their combination: მე წიგნს ვკითხულობ. me c'igns vk'itxulob. 'I am reading a book.'
The meaning is composed of: me 'I', c'igns 'book (DAT)', vk'itxulob 'read (1SG subject)'.

key_areas.name: Logical Form
examples: Quantifier scope: ყველა კაცი ვინმეს უყვარს. qvela k'ac'i vinmes uq'vars. 'Every man loves someone.' (ambiguous scope)
Binding: მან თავისი წიგნი წაიკითხა. man tavisi c'igni c'aik'itxa. 'He read his own book.'

key_areas.name: Quantifier Raising
examples: Quantifiers move to a higher position for scope interpretation.

key_areas.name: Binding Theory
examples: Reflexive: თავი tavi 'self' must be bound locally.
Pronoun: ის is 'he/she/it' must be free in its governing category.

Semantics-Pragmatics_Interface.definition: The interaction between literal meaning and context-dependent interpretation.

key_areas.name: Speech acts
examples: Assertion: ეს წიგნია. es c'ignia. 'This is a book.'
Question: ეს წიგნია? es c'ignia? 'Is this a book?'
Wish: ნეტავ მოვიდეს! netav movides! 'If only he would come!'

key_areas.name: Presupposition
examples: The fact that ... : ის ფაქტი, რომ ის მოვიდა, ყველას გააკვირვა. is p'ak'ti, rom is movida, qvelas gaakvirva. 'The fact that he came surprised everyone.'

key_areas.name: Implicature
examples: Scalar implicature: ზოგი მოვიდა. zogi movida. 'Some came.' (implicates: not all came)

key_areas.name: Reference resolution
examples: Pronouns: ის is 'he/she/it' refers to a contextually salient entity.

Phonology-Syntax_Interface.definition: The interaction between sound structure and sentence structure.
key_areas: Intonation and clause type: falling for statements, rising for yes/no questions.
Prosodic phrasing: syntactic constituents align with prosodic phrases.

Morphology-Pragmatics_Interface.definition: The interaction between word structure and context-dependent interpretation.
key_areas: Evidentiality: The Perfect screeve (with -ი-ა -i-a) indicates indirect evidentiality (apparently, hearsay).
Honorifics: Use of plural forms for polite address (თქვენ tkven 'you (PL)' for singular polite).

subject.definition: The syntactic subject of a clause. In Georgian, the subject is marked by nominative case in Series I and III (for intransitives), by ergative case in Series II (for transitives), and by dative case in Series III (for transitives).

examples.translation: I have apparently written a book.
examples.subject: მე me 'I' (DAT)

object.definition: The syntactic object of a clause. In Georgian, the direct object is marked by dative case in Series I, and by nominative case in Series II and III.

agent.definition: Semantic role of the doer of the action. Typically marked by ergative case in Series II and by nominative case in Series I.

patient.definition: Semantic role of the undergoer of the action. Typically marked by nominative case in Series II and by dative case in Series I.

experiencer.definition: Semantic role of the entity that experiences a psychological state. Typically marked by dative case with indirect verbs.

beneficiary.definition: Semantic role of the entity for whose benefit an action is performed. Typically marked by the postposition -თვის -tvis 'for' or by objective version in the verb.

instrument.definition: Semantic role of the entity used to perform an action. Typically marked by instrumental case.

location.definition: Semantic role of the place where an action occurs. Typically marked by locative case or postpositions.

examples.translation: The book is on the table.

goal.definition: Semantic role of the entity toward which an action is directed. Typically marked by dative case.

examples.translation: I am giving him/her the book.

source.definition: Semantic role of the entity from which an action originates. Typically marked by ablative case or postpositions.

possessor.definition: Semantic role of the entity that possesses something. Typically marked by genitive case.

precedes.definition: Linear order relation. In Georgian, subjects typically precede objects, and objects precede verbs (SOV).

allomorph.definition: Relation between a morpheme and its allomorphs.

allophone.definition: Relation between a phoneme and its phones.

examples.phrase: სწრაფად ვკითხულობ sc'rapad vk'itxulob 'I read quickly'
examples.head: ვკითხულობ vk'itxulob 'I read' (V)

argument.definition: The syntactic entity about which something is predicated.

realization.definition: Relation between a linguistic unit and its physical form.

semanticRole.definition: Relation between a participant and a predicate.

examples.entailment: მან წიგნი დაწერა. man c'igni dac'era. 'He wrote a book.' entails წიგნი არსებობს. c'igni arsebobs. 'A book exists.'

inLanguage.definition: Relation between a linguistic sign and the Georgian language.

phoneticRep.definition: Phonetic representation of a linguistic unit.

phonemicRep.definition: Phonemic representation of a linguistic unit.

orthographicRep.definition: Orthographic representation of a linguistic unit (Mkhedruli script).

gloss.definition: Gloss or translation of a linguistic unit.

hasExample.definition: Example usage of a linguistic unit.

examples.example: ეს სახლია. es saxl-ia. 'This is a house.'
წიგნს ვკითხულობ. c'igns vk'itxulob. 'I am reading a book.'

stringRep.definition: String representation of a linguistic unit.

agreement.definition: The verb agrees with subject, direct object, and indirect object through affixes.

government.definition: Postpositions and verbs determine case marking of noun phrases.

adjunct.definition: A phrase modifying a head but not an actant.

examples.clause: ხვალ მოვალ. xval moval. 'I will come tomorrow.'
სახლში ვკითხულობ. saxlši vk'itxulob. 'I read at home.'

apposition.definition: Two noun phrases juxtaposed referring to the same entity.

examples.clause: ნადირი, ჩემი მეგობარი, აქ ცხოვრობს. nadiri, č'emi megobari, ak cxovrobs. 'Nadiri, my friend, lives here.'
examples.apposition: ნადირი nadiri 'Nadiri' and ჩემი მეგობარი č'emi megobari 'my friend'

Lexicon_Overview.definition: The lexicon of Georgian includes native Kartvelian roots and extensive borrowings from Iranian, Arabic, Turkish, Russian, and European languages. The lexicon is characterized by complex morphology, including numerous derivational suffixes and prefixes, and a rich system of verbal roots with preverbs.
Lexicon_Overview.word_structure: Most words are disyllabic or monosyllabic; CV and CVC syllable structures are most common. However, complex consonant clusters (up to 6 consonants initially) are a hallmark of Georgian phonology.
Lexicon_Overview.loanwords: Primarily from Iranian (Old and Middle Persian), Arabic, Turkish, Russian, and European languages; adapt to Georgian phonotactic constraints and morphology.
Lexicon_Overview.noun_classes: Nouns are not classified by grammatical gender. Natural gender is expressed lexically (e.g., კაცი k'ac'i 'man' vs ქალი kali 'woman').
Lexicon_Overview.nominal_compounds: Highly productive; plural marked on the second constituent.

Relations_and_Properties_Summary.definition: Summary of the most important relations and properties in the Georgian language ontology.
key_relations: subject: The syntactic subject of a clause (nominative in Series I, ergative in Series II, dative in Series III for transitives).
object: The syntactic object of a clause (dative in Series I, nominative in Series II and III).
agent: The doer of the action (typically ergative in Series II, nominative in Series I).
patient: The undergoer of the action (typically nominative in Series II, dative in Series I).
experiencer: The entity experiencing a psychological state (typically dative with indirect verbs).
precedes: Linear order relation (Subject precedes Object precedes Verb).
allomorph: Relation between a morpheme and its allomorphs (e.g., -eb- vs -n- plural).
allophone: Relation between a phoneme and its phones (e.g., /p/ → [pʰ]).
head: The head of a phrase.
complement: Syntactic argument of a verb.
argument: The syntactic entity about which something is predicated.
realization: Relation between a linguistic unit and its physical form.
semanticRole: Relation between a participant and a predicate.
inLanguage: Relation between a linguistic sign and Georgian.

Typological_Summary.definition: A summary of the typological characteristics of Georgian.
Typological_Summary.alignment: Split ergative: Nominative-Accusative in Series I, Ergative-Absolutive in Series II, Inverted (Dative-Nominative) in Series III

phonology.vowels: 5 (a, e, i, o, u) - no length distinction
phonology.consonants: 28 - three-way laryngeal contrast (voiced, aspirated voiceless, ejective)
phonology.stress: Weak, dynamic, usually on the first syllable

verb_system.series_I: Present, Future, Imperfect, Conditional, Present Subjunctive, Future Subjunctive
verb_system.preverbs: 12+ directional prefixes (a-, ga-, da-, še-, ča-, c'a-, mi-, mo-, gada-, šemo-, gamo-, čamo-)

lexicon.native_roots: Kartvelian roots (e.g., saxli 'house', c'q'ali 'water', c'era 'to write')
lexicon.derivation: Rich system of suffixes and prefixes
